summary: For 5–6 year olds, the learning goal is a hands-on engineering-enquiry loop: set an observable goal, predict, test, record the outcome, read the record to judge whether the design met the goal, change ONE thing, and re-test. The teaching objective is first-hand building and testing with real ramps, marbles, launchers and targets, where the recorded evidence (not the child's wish or how fun it was) decides success — and a design that missed the goal is something to improve, not simply 'broken'. A screen 'design-test bench' is a strong proxy for the data-and-judgment logic but cannot provide the haptic build-and-test experience, so it belongs alongside real apparatus. Stay within the K-PS2-2 assessment boundary by changing speed with push strength or ramp height, and direction with push direction or a block/wall/curved track that turns the marble, not friction. The UK anchor is the Working Scientifically enquiry skill, not forces content, which is not in KS1.
misconceptions: Judging that the design 'worked' by intention or enjoyment ('I wanted it to, so it did' / 'it was fun, so it worked') rather than by the observed outcome against the goal.
Treating the goal vaguely so success can't be checked — no concrete, observable success criterion was set.
Changing several things at once between tries, so the child can't tell which change made the difference (emergent fair-testing gap at this age).
Expecting one try to settle it — not yet repeating the test or noticing run-to-run variation.

Carrying the 'motion needs a continuous force' intuition from Pushes & Pulls — thinking the object keeps a push 'inside it' (the impetus idea seeded young; keep the focus on the design test, not on explaining why it eventually stops, which is outside the K assessment boundary anyway).
Thinking a design that failed the goal is simply 'broken' rather than something to modify and improve (missing the iterate-and-improve idea).

activities.title: Real ramp-and-marble design test (primary hands-on investigation)
steps: Agree a concrete, observable goal together first, e.g. make the marble reach the teddy, knock down the cups, or follow a curved path round a barrier.
Before each release, say or point to what you think will happen (predict).
Roll the marble, then BEFORE deciding if it worked, record the outcome: mark on the mat/track where the marble stopped, or drop a hit/miss token or sticker onto a results strip.

Change only ONE thing between tries (higher OR lower ramp, harder OR gentler push, or, for a turning goal, moving a block/wall that steers the marble), re-test, and place the new record next to the last one.
Look back along the row of recorded stops and decide: did the design meet the goal? Pick the next change the records point to, and re-test to confirm.
Say out loud how you know it worked, using the marks and tokens as evidence.
activities.insight: A design 'works as intended' when the recorded outcome meets the agreed goal — the evidence decides, not what you hoped or how fun it was; changing one thing at a time lets you see what each change did, and a miss is something to change and try again.

activities.title: Screen 'design-test bench' (digital companion for the data-judgment logic)
steps: Set ONE thing on the ramp/launcher: drag the ramp height OR pull back a push slider, or, for the curve-path goal, place a wall/bumper that turns the marble (shown from above).
Tap to predict what will happen, then release the marble toward the goal target (reach the bear / knock cups / curve path).
Watch the bench leave a stop-mark where the marble stopped and drop a hit/miss token onto a results strip at the bottom.

After a few tries, read the filled results strip at a glance and see what it actually shows — for a reach-the-target goal, tries that are too gentle or too low may fall short, while tries that are too hard or too high may roll past.

Pick the change the evidence points to (higher ramp or harder push when it fell short; lower ramp or gentler push when it rolled past; move the wall when it went the wrong way) and re-test to confirm; the 'change one thing' lock greys out a second change until the first is tested.
activities.insight: Watching recorded outcomes accumulate and reading that strip to make a decision shows that the recorded data, not the wish, tells you whether the design works — and what one change to try next.

activities.title: Labelled scene vocabulary primer (reference layer)
steps: Tap parts of a static scene (ramp, marble, push arrow, goal) to reveal naming: 'this is a push', 'this is the ramp', 'this is our goal'.
Tap the ramp to reveal 'a ramp can make it go faster'; tap the goal to reveal the reflective prompt 'did the marble reach it?'
Lift a flap on 'how could we make it go further?' to reveal 'start it higher up — make the ramp higher'.
activities.insight: Reinforces the prerequisite push/pull words and names the parts of the test setup so the enquiry vocabulary is in place.

activities.title: Picture-and-audio judgment check (light consolidation)
steps: Answer an image-based question: 'Did the marble reach the bear? yes/no'.
Compare two pictures that each show where the marble stopped, and pick which ramp made it go further by looking at the stopping points.
Put the test steps in order: predict → test → look → decide.
activities.insight: Consolidates judging a design against an observed outcome and the order of the test loop, after the child has done real testing.

checkQuestion: Here is a little ramp and a marble. We want the marble to roll across the mat and STOP on the target circle. Have a go at making that happen. Try it a few times, watch what the marble does, then change something to get it closer to the target — and tell me what you changed and why.
checkAnswer: Rolls the marble and watches whether it overshoots, stops short, or lands on the target, then makes a purposeful change based on what happened — e.g. lower the ramp (or start gentler) if it overshoots, raise it if it stops short — and tries again, judging success by whether the marble lands closer. Links the change to the observed result (too far -> less push / lower ramp).
